conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and common after procedures. We’ll encourage deep breathing and suction as needed. It should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’m feeling sleepy and my breathing feels off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen is down to 85%. Let’s check your trach. Stay calm—we’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you oxygen and bagging through the trach. Your ABG shows very high CO2—119—and low pH. This is respiratory failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my trach out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s displaced. We’re taking you for an urgent bronchoscopy to reposition it. You’ll be sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back in your room. The bronchoscopy confirmed your trach had moved up. We replaced it and dilated the stenosis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it secure now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s sutured in place. You were on the ventilator briefly but are now off and breathing on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’ll be moved to the ICU for close monitoring tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re stable. A bedside bronchoscopy confirmed the trach is in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go back to the floor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once we wean you fully off the vent. You’re already breathing well on your trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on the floor. Your oxygen levels are stable on room air during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. How’s my heart? I saw monitors beeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a brief episode of atrial flutter—fast heart rhythm—but it resolved on its own and didn’t cause symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. Your echo showed strong heart function. We’ll check with cardiology about a monitor after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look much better. White count is down to 7.7, and your kidneys are fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My pain is better with oxycodone every 4 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that as needed. You’re also on Tylenol and ibuprofen. No signs of sedation, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your trach shifted slightly again—about 1 cm out. We did another bedside bronchoscopy and adjusted it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? Why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tissue is fragile from repeated procedures. This time we used a shorter Portex tube and redilated the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it stable now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll monitor closely. You’ve been off the vent since yesterday and are breathing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another dilation today to keep the airway open. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How often will I need these?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monthly for now. Your pulmonologist will coordinate. We’re also following up on a biopsy from earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your TSH came back normal, so the arrhythmia isn’t thyroid-related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t always find a cause. It could be from stress on your system. Since your stroke risk is low, we won’t start blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I get my tobramycin nebs at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on that. Your pharmacy hasn’t stocked it. We’ll help you get it sorted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see pulmonology for your next bronchoscopy and rheumatology for your relapsing polychondritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your breathing is stable, labs are normal, and you’re alert and comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you tomorrow. You’ll take oxycodone for pain, and all your other meds continue as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heart monitor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange a 30-day event monitor. Call if you feel palpitations or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your trach is secure, and you’re maintaining oxygen on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep using your duonebs, Esbriet, and nebulized tobramycin. Call if you have breathing trouble or trach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge summary says you were admitted because the trach was out of position and you had trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s accurate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we fixed it with bronchoscopy and repositioning. You’re on your way to recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lucky to have such a good team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re doing well. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember to keep your trach secure and the neck strap snug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll check it often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And use your home trach mask at night as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay safe and healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You're here for monitoring after your bronchoscopy and airway dilation today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m okay. My breathing feels normal, like my usual baseline. But my trach site is a bit sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You had dilation of both your left and right mainstem bronchi today, which can cause some localized discomfort. There was just a little oozing, and we gave you some medicine to prevent swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I get these every four weeks. But I’m glad the procedure went smoothly. Last time, the trach got displaced and I ended up in the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I reviewed your history. That was a scary moment, but you recovered well. This time, your trach is secure, and your oxygen levels are excellent—99% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Should I be worried about breathing problems this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. Your lungs are moving well, and we’ll keep monitoring you. We did a chest X-ray after the procedure to make sure there’s no air leak or collapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lung volumes are a bit low, which is common after sedation, but no pneumothorax. There’s some stable atelectasis on the right side, which we’ve seen before. Nothing new or concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. My chest pain is mostly at the trach site, not deep in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s consistent with post-procedure soreness. We’ll manage that with pain medication. You’re on acetaminophen and ibuprofen regularly, and oxycodone if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d prefer to avoid the oxycodone if I can. I’ve used it before, but I don’t like how it makes me feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely fine. We’ll stick with Tylenol and ibuprofen first. Let us know if the pain gets worse, especially with breathing or swallowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your labs from this morning. Your white blood cell count was a bit high last night—14.2—but it’s come down to 7.6 today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that from infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It’s common after a procedure like this. The inflammation from the dilation can raise the count temporarily. With no fever or other signs, we don’t think it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My stomach’s been a little off too—could that be from the Esbriet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your team has noted that your GERD symptoms may be related to Esbriet. We’re keeping you on both famotidine and pantoprazole to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll keep taking those. How long will I need to stay this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually, patients like you stay 2–3 days for pain control after dilation. Since you’re doing well, we’re hoping to discharge you day after tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I have another dilation scheduled in four weeks, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and there’s also a plan to place a custom trach at that time. We’ll coordinate that with your ENT and pulmonology teams.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The ibuprofen helps. I only took one dose of oxycodone last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your breathing sounds are improving too—just faint wheezes now, no rales. We’ll keep encouraging deep breathing and coughing to keep your lungs clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing the incentive spirometer every hour like they showed me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That helps prevent atelectasis, especially with your history. Your blood pressure is stable too—110 over 65 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my losartan every day. Should I adjust the dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, stay on your usual dose. We’re monitoring it, and it’s well-controlled. We’ll keep you on all your home meds except adjusting pain management as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs this morning are stable. Your bicarbonate is a bit high at 30, but that’s likely from mild chronic respiratory retention, not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my lung condition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from long-standing airway disease and fibrosis. But your oxygen levels are strong, so we’re not concerned. Your kidney and liver functions are normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? Still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re breathing comfortably at rest, rate of 18, saturating 99% on trach collar. We’ll do a final check tomorrow, and if all stays well, you can go home in the afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll need to refill the pain meds, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send prescriptions for acetaminophen and ibuprofen—both 10 days’ supply. The oxycodone is still available if needed, but we encourage using it sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll follow up with my pulmonologist after the next procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning! You’re looking well. Final exam shows your trach site is clean, no bleeding. Lungs are clear with just a little wheeze. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any instructions before I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your regular medications, including Esbriet, inhalers, and blood pressure pill. Use the pain meds as scheduled for the next few days. Watch for fever, increased pain, or breathing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the trach ever comes out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call 911 or go to the ER immediately. But your trach is stable now, and we’ve reinforced the ties. You’ve been through this before—you know the signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. Thanks for taking good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're here today for your scheduled bronchoscopy and tracheostomy tube replacement, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's right. I come in every month for the dilation because of the narrowing in my airway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Given your Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome and relapsing polychondritis, these monthly procedures help keep your airway open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. Last time, things got a little scary with the unresponsiveness. I hope that doesn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring you closely. The procedure went smoothly today. No complications during the bronchoscopy or balloon dilation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I do feel some soreness around the trach site, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’ll manage your pain with acetaminophen and ibuprofen. If it’s still uncomfortable, we can give you oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I usually only need it the first day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it on hand. Also, we tried placing your custom trach tube today, but it got compressed, so we used a standard Portex 9 instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I remember that from last time. Is it safe to keep the Portex for now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s perfectly safe. We’ll plan for another attempt at the custom tube in a few weeks, once we reassess the anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the dilation—did it help open up the blockages?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We dilated the distal trachea up to 10 mm, the left mainstem to 9 mm, and the right side to 8 mm. There was some granulation tissue, which we gently removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tissue was very fragile, but we controlled any minor bleeding with topical epinephrine. You’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had issues with suctioning before—caused bleeding. I’d prefer to avoid that if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll rely on your cough to clear secretions unless absolutely necessary. Your lungs sound clear for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray from yesterday shows the trach is in place, no pneumothorax, and lung volumes have improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. How’s my breathing looking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on 40% oxygen via trach mask, saturating at 100%. No signs of distress. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my inhalers less. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on scheduled tobramycin and fluticasone. I noticed you said you haven’t been using them regularly at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forget sometimes. And the tobramycin wasn’t filled last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important for preventing infections, especially with your history of Pseudomonas and other bacteria. Please restart it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I have an ID follow-up soon, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with Dr. ___ this month. They’ll help keep your airway infections under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray this morning shows no changes—trach is stable, no fluid or collapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was a bit high yesterday—11.5—but it’s down to 8.5 today. That’s a good sign, no infection brewing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My cough and shortness of breath at home haven’t changed, which is normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your baseline is chronic cough and dyspnea. As long as it’s not worsening, we’re on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. Pain is minimal, you’re off supplemental oxygen, and walking around fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all stays stable. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll go home with a small supply of oxycodone for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just for a day or two?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, six tablets total—10 mg every four hours as needed. But stick to Tylenol and ibuprofen if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I continue all my other meds—Esbriet, prednisone, losartan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. All your home medications are continued—Esbriet, prednisone, losartan, pantoprazole, and the inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And rheumatology follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with Dr. ___ to monitor your relapsing polychondritis. They’ll coordinate the next bronchoscopy in four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Final check—your vitals are stable, lungs still clear, and you’re breathing comfortably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m cleared to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue all medications, avoid trach suctioning unless absolutely necessary, and follow up with rheumatology and ID.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my breathing gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your team or go to the ER. But you’ve been stable post-procedure, so we expect continued improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I feel much better than last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—your discharge paperwork is ready. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll get set up to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we discussed the plan for a possible stent in the left mainstem bronchus in the future. That’s still on the table.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember. They measured it this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 4 cm in length. We’re considering an 8x40 or 10x30 stent later if needed. But for now, monthly dilation is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know. I’ll keep that in mind for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your father is listed as your contact. We’ve gone over the discharge instructions with him too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’ll help me at home. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, just one more question—should I worry if I cough up a little blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Minor streaking can happen due to the friable tissue. If it’s more than a few streaks or lasts more than a day, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're here tonight for your scheduled bronchoscopy to dilate your airway and replace your tracheostomy tube. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doctor. I’m okay, a little nervous. My breathing’s been tighter lately, so I guess this is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The tightness is due to the tracheal stenosis from your Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome and relapsing polychondritis. The procedure tomorrow will help open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, we’ve done this before. But last time, the custom tube didn’t fit. Will that happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll assess during the procedure. If needed, we’ll use a standard tube like last time. The main goal is to dilate the trachea and bronchi safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the pain afterward? Last time I needed oxycodone for a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your pain meds available—acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and oxycodone as needed. You may feel some soreness at the trach site, but we’ll manage it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ll rest up tonight then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re up early. How’d you sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not bad. A bit stiff, but I’m ready to get this done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The procedure is scheduled for 9 AM. We’ll dilate your trachea to 12 mm, right bronchus to 8 mm, and left to 10 mm. We’ll also take washings to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be out for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be under sedation. And afterward, you might be on the ventilator briefly just to help with pain control while you wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? That was weird, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll monitor you closely. Your vitals are stable now—heart rate 100, BP 99/55, oxygen at 99% on 40% trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re back in your room. The procedure went well—no complications. We dilated as planned and replaced the trach tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel groggy. Was I on the vent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about an hour. Just to help with pain while you came around. You’re now on the trach mask and breathing comfortably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any issues with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We used a standard Portex 9 again—the custom one didn’t fit due to compression. But it’s secure and working fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as last time. Okay. How’s my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lungs are clear on exam. The chest X-ray shows no pneumothorax or fluid. Lung volumes were low earlier but improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the washings? Any sign of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sent to lab, but no results yet. We’ll follow up if anything comes back. Your white count is 13.6, a bit high, but that’s likely from inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been on steroids for years—does that affect healing?
